summary: Sets the architectural assumptions for mapping between SIP and XMPP, two protocols used for messaging and presence. It also specifies how addresses and error conditions are mapped between the two. It is the foundation for other mapping documents.

plainLanguage.summary: Two chat systems speak different languages. This document sets the basic ground rules, like how names and error messages are translated from one to the other.

subtitle: The ground rules for translating between SIP and XMPP: where gateways sit, how addresses map, and how errors map.

tldr.problem: SIP and XMPP are both widely deployed for messaging, presence and real-time sessions, but their addresses and error signals differ, so systems built on one cannot talk to the other directly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assumes a dedicated gateway translates directly between the protocols, and defines rules for mapping the local part and instance part of addresses and tables mapping XMPP error conditions to SIP response codes and back.
tldr.outcome: It is the foundation of a series of SIP-XMPP mapping documents (presence, messaging, media sessions), and the mappings are suggestions that implementations may deviate from.

sections.title: Why SIP and XMPP Need Mappings
sections.content:
Two IETF signaling technologies can carry multimedia session negotiation, instant messaging, presence and notifications: the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261) with its SIMPLE extensions, and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP, RFC 6120). Because both are widely deployed, the RFC says it is important to define mappings between them.

This document is the basis for a series. It covers architectural assumptions, address translation and error mapping; other documents in the series cover presence, messaging and media sessions. The guidance comes from implementation and deployment experience, and it describes direct protocol mappings rather than mapping through an abstract model such as RFC 3859 and RFC 3860.

The audience is developers with an existing system on one technology who want it to reach systems on the other. Readers are assumed to know the core specifications for both.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people use one chat app and some use another. This document is the start of a guide for building a bridge between them.

sections.title: Gateway Architecture
sections.content:
Translation could happen in a multiprotocol server, in a multiprotocol client, or in a gateway that is a dedicated protocol translator. This document assumes a gateway. Information flowing from XMPP to SIP is translated by an XMPP-to-SIP gateway acting for an XMPP server (together an XMPP service). Information flowing from SIP to XMPP is translated by a SIP-to-XMPP gateway acting for a SIP server.

For the examples, the gateway is assumed to sit in the source domain, inside the trust domain of the user who generated the information. The RFC does not recommend against translation at the destination domain. The two logical functions can be one actual entity, and the gateway assumption is not meant to discourage translation inside multiprotocol clients or servers.

Communication between the servers can run over either protocol. If the XMPP user starts the exchange, the XMPP server invokes its XMPP-to-SIP gateway and the traffic uses SIP. If the SIP user starts it, the SIP server invokes its SIP-to-XMPP gateway and the traffic uses XMPP.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a translator who stands next to the person who starts talking and turns what they say into the other language.

sections.title: Interdomain Federation
sections.content:
A SIP system and an XMPP system communicate by interdomain federation. The SIP server uses its gateway to talk to the XMPP server with native XMPP server-to-server methods, and the XMPP server uses its gateway to talk to the SIP server with native SIP server-to-server methods.

An XMPP server that gets a stanza for another domain first does DNS SRV lookups for _xmpp-server records as specified in RFC 6120. If a hostname comes back it tries XMPP; if not, it finds the SIP location using the procedures of RFC 3263. A SIP server does the reverse: it tries the RFC 3263 procedures first and falls back to the _xmpp-server SRV lookup. Caching what a server has learned is left to implementations and local policy.

Existing SIP and XMPP servers do not typically speak the other protocol, so a common pattern is to attach a gateway to the core server. Because RFC 6120 binds XMPP to TCP, a SIP-to-XMPP gateway needs TCP. SIP can use TCP or UDP, and a deployment might support only UDP, so an XMPP-to-SIP gateway might need either.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending a letter, a server looks up which language the other building speaks, and if it is not its own, it hands the letter to its translator.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content:
SIP addresses are normally sip or sips URIs, and may be im or pres URIs when instant messaging or presence extensions are used. XMPP addresses follow RFC 6122. The RFC maps the form user@domain, focusing on the local part, plus the instance-specific part. Telephone numbers and domain names (including internationalized names) are out of scope.

The three schemes allow different characters, so characters allowed in one but not another must be escaped. When transforming a local part an application SHOULD: unescape the source address, leave characters allowed in the destination alone, and escape characters allowed in the source but reserved in the destination. Where the destination is a URI, the character MUST be percent-encoded (for example, the hash character becomes %23). Where it is a native XMPP address it MUST be encoded as \hexhex per XEP-0106 (' becomes \27).

For devices, an XMPP resourcepart (the part of a JID after the slash) matches a SIP GRUU, so the gr URI parameter maps to the resourcepart and back. This does not apply to temporary GRUUs. Non-ASCII characters need percent-encoding because the gr parameter holds only ASCII.

From SIP to XMPP, the steps are: remove the scheme, split at the first @, percent-decode, treat the result as UTF-8, translate &, ' and / to \26, \27 and \2f, optionally apply Nodeprep, recombine into a bare JID, and append / plus any gr value. From XMPP to SIP the steps are broadly the reverse, choosing im or pres if the foreign domain supports them and otherwise sip or sips according to local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Names are written with different rules in each system. Any letter that is not allowed gets swapped for a special code on the way over, and swapped back at the other end.

sections.title: Error Mapping
sections.content:
The RFC says error mapping is "more of an art than a science". XMPP has a fixed set of stanza error conditions (22 in RFC 6120), while SIP response codes are more numerous (71 registered with IANA at the time of writing) and often more specific. SIP also separates responses about one endpoint (4xx) from responses about a whole user (6xx), which XMPP does not. The tables are suggestions and implementations are free to deviate. Only the SIP 3xx, 4xx, 5xx and 6xx families are mapped, since XMPP has nothing like 1xx or 2xx.

For XMPP to SIP, the mapping SHOULD follow Table 2. Examples: <bad-request/> maps to 400, <not-authorized/> to 401, <internal-server-error/> to 500, and <redirect/> to 302. Several have two choices that depend on whether the error concerns a full JID or a bare JID. <gone/> MUST become 301 if it carries a new address and 410 if not.

For SIP to XMPP, Table 3 applies. Unlisted codes fall back by family: 3xx to <redirect/>, 4xx to <bad-request/>, 5xx to <internal-server-error> and 6xx to <recipient-unavailable/>. Mapping 301 to <gone/> MUST include the new address, and mapping 410 MUST NOT.

XMPP <service-unavailable/> is not mapped to SIP 503. The 503 code means a server is unreachable for all future requests, which differs from the XMPP meaning, so that mapping is NOT RECOMMENDED. SIP 403 and 405 are the closest in meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, each system has its own set of error messages. The translator picks the closest match, like choosing the nearest word in another language.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Gateways SHOULD use TLS over TCP and DTLS over UDP when talking to the other side. Detailed security considerations for SIP and XMPP are in RFC 3261 and RFC 6120.

A sips URI in the To header or Request-URI means every hop needs TLS protection. XMPP cannot signal that, so a SIP-to-XMPP gateway MUST NOT translate such a message into an XMPP stanza or route it to the XMPP server (barring rare explicit agreements between operators).

A gateway effectively acts as a SIP back-to-back user agent (B2BUA), which can expose the amplification vulnerability described in RFC 5393. Gateways SHOULD implement loop-detection methods for it, but defenses against looping between SIP and XMPP networks are otherwise out of scope. The wide Unicode range also invites confusion over look-alike characters in identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message asked for a locked, safe route all the way, the translator must not pass it to a route that cannot promise that.
